Case Report A 56-year-old women presented with a 6-month history of increasing muscle cramps and stiffness of both legs, trunk, and inability to walk independently, and a 10-kg weight loss (see Video). There was no weakness in the legs or arms, pyramidal signs were negative, and cranial nerves were normal. EMG (Fig. 1A) revealed involuntary continuous motor unit activity (CMUA) in all affected muscles, including the truncal muscles, without evidence for reflex spasms elicited by acoustic stimuli and electrical peripheral nerve stimulation. Nerve conduction studies were normal. Central motor conduction as measured by transcranial magnetic stimulation to both arms and legs wasnormal, arguing against this being a spastic syndrome. Laboratory results were negative for GAD antibodies but antiamphiphysin antibodies were highly increased (1: 409, 600), Given a normal mammogram and thoracic/abdominal CAT scan, a whole-body 18F-fluorodesoxyglucose (FDG) PET was performed, showing two extracranial areas of increased FDG uptake retrosternal and adjacent to the right pulmonary hilus (Fig. 1B). An additional area of increased FDG uptake surrounded by a decreased uptake was detected in central regions of the right frontal lobe (Fig. 1C), later confirmed by MRI suggesting metastasis. Histology following exstirpation of the structure within the right frontal lobe confirmed metastasis of a small cell lung carcinoma. Symptomatic treatment of SPS was initiated with benzodiazepines and corticosteroids followed by causal cancer therapy with cisplatin/etoposid and radiotherapy, which led to a remarkable improvement of mobility during the followingmonths. The patient was able to walk independently for short distances and stiffness was significantly reduced (see Video). Discussion This case presented with a typical history and clinical picture of SPS, confirmed by EMG. The rapid progression combined with positive antiamphiphysin antibodies was suggestive of a paraneoplastic disorder, which in SPS is usually associated with breast cancer. Our case shows that small cell lung cancer should be ruled out in patients with an antiamphiphysin /H11001SPS if there is no evidence for breast cancer. As in our case, GAD antibodies are typically negative in antiamphiphysin /H11001paraneoplastic SPS. 7 Antiamphiphysin antibodies are a useful screening tool for a presumed paraneoplastic neurological syndrome since they are rarely found in patients with cancer without a neurological deficit. However, they are not specific and may be associated with a variety of different neurological syndromes and tumors (Table 1). 4, 5 Legends to the Video Segment 1.
